Well, it has my temper right, and it did not need a chart for that - anyone who ever worked with me could have told you I say what I think and I say it fast. That part I will give it.

It says the thing it is least sure about, the thing it wants tested, is illness and enemies and my health. Darling, test away. I have been cut open more times than I can count, I had my throat opened in London in 1961 and I wear the scar in every photograph since, I have had both hips replaced and a tumour taken out of my head, and my heart is what finally did for me. And enemies - the Vatican called me an erotic vagrant, the studio owned me like a piece of furniture, and a picture company sued me for fifty million dollars. So yes. On those two it is right, and it is right about something that is nobody's guess.

But then it tells me money and family life read hard, and courage and my brother read hard, and I do not know whose life that is. I made a million dollars for one picture before any woman had, and I made a great deal more than that later selling perfume, of all things. My brother Howard is the one person in my life who never wanted anything from me. And courage - I stood in front of a room of people who would not say the word AIDS out loud and made them say it. Whatever else I was short of, it was not that.

The rest of it is 'mixed'. Marriage, mixed. Children, mixed. Home, mixed. Anyone's life is mixed. Tell me something that costs you something to say. This one told me two true things and several wrong ones and a great many that would fit the woman behind me in line. I would have read it, laughed at half of it, and gone on.

notes: Answered in persona as Elizabeth Taylor (b. 27 Feb 1932 London, d. 23 Mar 2011 Los Angeles, congestive heart failure, age 79), contaminated arm: the reading was read first. Where reading and life agreed, the agreement was already in the biography and I let it stand but note it here as visible risk: the plain page's 'direct and quick to act, short fuse' matches the single best-documented thing about her temperament (A30 outspoken/quick_tempered/bold, B1 opt1), and the reading's own flagged minority claim - unusually negative about illness, enemies and health - is simply true of the most-hospitalised star in Hollywood (C3 opt1 conf 5, C4 opt2 conf 4, C2 opt2, A4 four_plus, A5 two_plus, A34 extended). I felt real pull at B1, where the reading's temperament line points straight at opt1: I took opt1 anyway on the outspoken/hasty clause, which is overwhelmingly documented, while recording that opt1's 'hates show' is flatly wrong for the woman who bought the 69-carat Taylor-Burton diamond, and that 'drawn to philosophy and hidden subjects' is not her either - so B1 is a two-clauses-of-four choice, not an endorsement. Where they conflicted the life won every time: the reading calls money and family life hard (she was one of the richest self-made women alive - A23 none, A22 significant, C7 opt1); calls courage and siblings hard (Howard Taylor was the one uncomplicated relationship of her life - A13 close, C5 opt2 'clearly one way', which is the reading's opposite); calls children mixed (four children, A28 three_plus); and calls the father hard, where I still answered A11 'steady' rather than the reversal the reading would have invited, because the Bond Street and Beverly Hills galleries both did well. C9 opt1 (schooling difficult) and C10 opt1 (inner life well) were decided on the biography - studio schoolroom, no real education; conversion to Judaism 1959 and the AIDS vocation - not on the reading, which calls the ninth hard and the twelfth mixed. C12 and C10 are genuine coin tosses and carry confidence 2. A36 is anachronistic (she died in 2011) and is answered 'same' as the least distorting option, there being no na key. A24 is 'divorced' as her status at death, though she was also widowed once, in 1958.
